'''Muniche''' is an extinct language which was spoken in the village of Munichis, about 10 miles (16 km) west of [[Yurimaguas]], [[Loreto Region]], [[Peru]]. The last known fluent speaker, Victoria Huancho Icahuate, died in the late 1990s, but the language was already moribund by the 1930s. As of 2009, there were several semi-speakers who retained significant lexical, and partial grammatical, knowledge of the language.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last=Michael |first=Lev |title=18 Muniche |date=2023-01-16 |work=Language Isolates II: Kanoé to Yurakaré |pages=851–892 |editor-last=Epps |editor-first=Patience |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9783110432732-005/html |access-date=2025-09-17 |publisher=De Gruyter |doi=10.1515/9783110432732-005 |isbn=978-3-11-043273-2 |last2=Farmer |first2=Stephanie |last3=Finley |first3=Gregory |last4=Acosta |first4=Karina Sullón |last5=Beier |first5=Christine |last6=Icahuate |first6=Alexandra Chanchari |last7=Baneo |first7=Donalia Icahuate |last8=Saita |first8=Melchor Sinti |editor2-last=Michael |editor2-first=Lev|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

It is also called ''Balsapuertiño'', named after the village of [[Balsa Puerto District|Balsapuerto]] in the [[department of Loreto]], Peru.<ref name="Loukotka">{{cite book |last=Loukotka |first=Čestmír |author-link=Čestmír Loukotka |title=Classification of South American Indian languages |url=https://archive.org/details/classificationof0007louk |url-access=registration |publisher=UCLA Latin American Center |year=1968 |location=Los Angeles}}</ref>

Word order in Muniche is [[Verb–subject–object|VSO]].<ref>Gibson, Michael Luke. 1996. ''El Munichi: Un idioma que se extingue''. (Serie Lingüística Peruana, 42.) Pucallpa: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. 103pp.</ref><ref>Michael Gibson. 1988. ''The Muniche Language: with partial reference to verb morphology''. (MA thesis, University of Reading).</ref>

==Classification==
The language is considered an isolate (Michael et al. 2013), but the [[pronominal]] [[suffixes]] bear a close resemblance to those reconstructed for proto-[[Arawakan]] (Gibson 1996:18-19), and some lexical items are similar to ones in Arawakan languages (Jolkesky 2016:310–317).<ref>Jolkesky, Marcelo Pinho De Valhery. 2016. ''[https://repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/21671 Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220122152416/https://www.repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/21671 |date=2022-01-22 }}''. Doutorado em Linguística. Universidade de Brasília.</ref> Although Jolkesky (''id''.) argues that the language belongs to a putative [[Macro-Arawakan languages|Macro-Arawakan]] stock, evidence has yet to be provided for placing it either in a sister branch to the Arawakan language family or in a branch within this language family. There is substantial borrowing from the local variety of [[Quechua languages|Quechua]], and to a lesser extent from [[Spanish language|Spanish]] and [[Cahuapanan languages]] (Michael et al. 2013).

==Varieties==
Currently, there are two distinguished varieties of Muniche. One of the dialects merges certain phonemes that the other dialect does not.<ref name=":0" />

== Language contact ==
Jolkesky (2016) notes that there are lexical similarities with the [[Hibito–Cholon languages|Cholon-Hibito]], [[Kechua languages|Kechua]], and [[Mochika language|Mochika]] language families due to contact.<ref name="Jolkesky-2016">{{cite thesis|last=Jolkesky |first=Marcelo Pinho de Valhery |date=2016 |url=http://www.etnolinguistica.org/tese:jolkesky-2016-arqueoecolinguistica |title=Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas |type=Ph.D. dissertation |location=Brasília |publisher=University of Brasília |edition=2}}</ref>

A number of Spanish loanwords may have passed through [[Shiwilu language|Shiwilu]], a [[Cahuapanan languages|Cahuapanan language]].<ref name=":0" />

== Phonology ==

=== Vowels ===
Munichi has six vowels: /a, e, i, ɨ, o, u/.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://linguistics.berkeley.edu/~saphon|title=SAPhon – South American Phonological Inventories|website=linguistics.berkeley.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-08-12}}</ref>
Michael et al. (2023) reduce this to five vowels, these being {{IPA|/i, ɨ, u, e, a/}}.<ref name=":0" />

=== Phonotactics ===
The maximal syllable in Muniche is C<sub>1</sub>C<sub>2</sub>VC<sub>3</sub>, with the following restrictions for the consonants. Syllables without onset are permitted.<ref name=":0" />

# C<sub>1</sub> must be voiceless.
# C<sub>2</sub> cannot be a fricative.
# C<sub>1</sub> and C<sub>2</sub> cannot be a glottal stop.
# C<sub>1</sub> and C<sub>2</sub> cannot be both fricatives or both affricates.

Many consonant clusters in Muniche are suspected to arise from vowel reduction.

== Verbs ==

=== Desiderative ===
Muniche has a [[desiderative]] suffix {{Lang|myr|-çu}} ~ {{Lang|myr|-cu}}, used to express that the subject of a verb to which the suffix is attached desires the outcome of the clause.<ref name=":0" />
{{Interlinear
| 1 = ʂa-çu-me=ɲe iʔteʔsira maçu
| 2 = eat-DESI-PFV=1SG soup deer
| 3 = 'I want to eat deer soup'
}}{{Interlinear
| 1 = çawɨ-çu=nɨ raneʔe
| 2 = sit-DESI-1SG there
| 3 = 'I want to sit there'
}}
The subject must be the one desiring the realization of an action and the realizer of the action. To express the desire of someone else realizing an action, the complement-taking verb {{Lang|myr|açta}} must be used.
{{Interlinear
| 1 = açta-me=ɲe sica-t=pɨ=nɨ puʔu ʂnɨrɨ
| 2 = want-PFV-1SG sell-IRR=2SG=1SG meat [[paca]]
| 3 = 'I want you to sell me paca meat'
}}
